english: One more penalty. If Gonzalo Montiel scores it, Argentina is world champion.

In the center circle, their captain waits, arms around his teammates. He is thirty-five. He lost four finals with his country, and six years earlier he said he was leaving the national team. This final in Qatar is perhaps his last chance.
As Montiel runs up, the captain looks at the sky. The same sky he points to after almost every goal, for his grandmother.
Twenty-five years earlier, a doctor in Rosario saw that this boy was barely growing. So every night he pricked his leg with a needle.

Almost four years after that final in Qatar, Argentina played another World Cup final. Two days later, he sat down to write a short note. In it there were two words. Me vacié (I emptied myself). He had given everything.

He was never one to talk much. He just played. How did a quiet and so small boy end up carrying a whole country? It all started on a little pitch in Rosario, one afternoon when a children's team was one player short.
In that note he also thanked his family: without them, he would not have had a career. And the first to believe in him was his grandmother.
It was a little neighbourhood club called Grandoli, in Rosario, Argentina. The coach, Salvador Aparicio, was looking for someone who could play.
Next to the pitch stood a woman, Celia. She had come to watch her grandson Matías, and she also had the little brother with her, four or five years old.
She pointed at the little one. The coach looked at him and hesitated. The boy was tiny, much smaller than the others. But Celia did not give up. She asked him again and again to let him play.
In the end, Aparicio agreed. He put him on the wing, right next to Celia, and told her: if he cries, take him off.

At first he barely touched the ball. But when it came to him again, he took it with his left foot and went past one boy after another. He did not cry. Years later, he remembered scoring two goals that day.
That afternoon, the other boys were two or three years older than him. Some were twice his size. It did not seem to matter.
Aparicio never took him off again. And from that day, it was Celia who took him to every training session and every match.

That boy was Lionel Andrés Messi. He was born in Rosario on the twenty-fourth of June 1987, the third child of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother was also called Celia, like his grandmother. His father worked in a steel plant. His mother, in a small magnet workshop.
He had two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Later, a little sister, María Sol, completed the family.
Rosario is a working-class city on the Paraná River, with factories, a port and two clubs that divide it: Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.

The family lived in a humble house in La Bajada, a neighbourhood in the south. With his brothers he played in the street until it got dark. Lionel was always the smallest, and always the one with the ball.

He went to a public school a few streets from home, School Number 66. Many years later, a mural with his face appeared in the neighbourhood. It says he is from another galaxy, and from this neighbourhood.
At home, everyone called him Leo. Later, because he was so small and so fast, his family and teammates gave him another name. La Pulga.
His mother said that at home he could be cheeky and stubborn. He hated losing, even at cards. But on the pitch, because of that stubbornness he never gave a ball up for lost.
His father and brothers supported Newell's Old Boys, the red-and-black half of the city. On match days, they all went to the stadium together. Leo already knew where he wanted to play.
At six he joined Newell's Old Boys, his family's club. In one of his first matches they won six-nil, and he scored four.
The boys born in 1987 formed a team that people in Rosario still talk about. They called it "La Máquina del '87". For years, they almost never lost.
Sometimes, opponents asked for a deal before kick-off: if it reached six-nil, the match would end. Even so, Lionel got angry if he had not scored himself.

One of his coaches, Carlos Marconi, has told it many times. He promised Leo an alfajor, a chocolate sweet, for every goal. Leo scored so many that Marconi changed the deal: two alfajores, but only for headers. Soon, the smallest on the pitch scored a header. He looked at Marconi smiling and held up two fingers.
His teammates remember details. Before playing, he cleaned his boots and taped his ankles, like a professional. He was eight or nine.
A teammate remembers a derby against Rosario Central. Leo beat the same defender again and again, until the boy's father shouted from the stands: hit him.
The league kept count of his goals: more than two hundred in five years. In Rosario they say it was many more.
His size was a problem. The bigger boys kicked him, and some parents shouted to stop him any way they could. He always got up and asked for the ball again.
His coaches wanted to protect him: they asked him to release the ball earlier. He kept dribbling. If he lost it, he went straight to win it back.
But in 1998, when he was ten, his grandmother Celia died. The one who had brought him to football was gone.
Years later, he said she was a very great love and that even today it is hard for him to talk about her. He dedicates his goals to her. After many of them, he looks up and points to the sky.
His mother said that, after Celia died, the boy talked to his grandmother and asked her for help. He told few people. He was not one to talk about his feelings.
Without her, he kept playing. He was still the best in his team. But something else was wrong, and everyone could see it. While the other boys grew, he did not.
Newell's took him to a hormone specialist, Diego Schwarzstein. The club wanted to know why its best youth player was so short.
Tests showed he lacked growth hormone. Without treatment, he would be ten or fifteen centimetres shorter than he should be.
One word would follow him for years. Small. The best player of his age in Rosario, and the smallest.
There was a treatment: a small injection in the legs, every night. It was very expensive, more than nine hundred dollars a month.
As a child, he learned to inject himself. Every night, the same routine: a needle in his own leg. A teammate remembers him doing it before playing, as if it were nothing.
A friend's father taught him to drive on a country road. Lionel was eleven.

Every month, his father did the sums. The medicine took a large part of his factory wage. Help from insurance and the club did not last. Without treatment, his son's football would end before it began.
So they looked for a club that would pay. Around that time, Lionel had a trial at River Plate, in Buenos Aires, one of the country's big clubs.
In 2026, Messi told it himself. He trained there about ten days, and River wanted him to stay. They even offered to pay for his treatment. But first, Newell's had to release him.
He was never so close to playing for a big club in his country.
But when they went back to Newell's to ask for his release, they refused, and River's offer vanished. That was the end of it, he said. Then help came from across the ocean.

An Argentine agent in Barcelona was receiving videos of a boy from Rosario. With another agent, he showed them to the club, and Barcelona invited him to a trial. In September 2000, Lionel and his father flew to Spain. He was thirteen.
At Newell's they did not know where he was. They were told he was ill.
There he played against older boys. The sporting director, Carles Rexach, went to watch him.
As the story goes, it should have taken Rexach three or four minutes from his seat to the pitch. It took fifteen: he could not stop watching the boy.
One of the boys was Cesc Fàbregas, Messi's future teammate for years. A coach asked him to mark the new Argentine, and mark him hard.
Cesc saw him so small he thought it would be easy. Seconds later he was on the ground, and the little Argentine was going off with the ball.
Rexach said he told the club: sign the boy, don't even think about it. But his bosses hesitated. He was foreign, very small and needed expensive treatment. Weeks passed and no one decided anything.
For Jorge, the wait was terrible. He had left a secure job at the factory. He lived with his son in a hotel, far from his country, not knowing whether they would have a home there.
After more than two months of waiting, Jorge called Rexach and was clear: if it was not settled soon, they would go back home.
On the fourteenth of December 2000, Rexach met the agents at a tennis club. With no paper at hand, he wrote a promise on a napkin: Barcelona would sign Lionel Messi.
Joan Gaspart, a club director, admitted the napkin was legally worthless. It was to calm a father about to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed, and the agents as witnesses. Years later, the napkin was auctioned in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
The club would pay for the treatment and give his father a job. In February 2001, the whole family moved to Spain.
At thirteen, Leo did not fully understand all that. He only knew he would play, and that the injections would continue, now paid for by Barça.
For the boy from La Bajada, it was a dream. For his family, the start of the hardest year of their lives.
Nothing went as they expected. Because of the rules for foreigners, he spent months without playing official matches. And in his second youth match, he broke his leg.
His mother, his brothers and his little sister missed home. They did not adapt, and within a year they decided to go back to Rosario.
Jorge asked his son if he wanted to go back. Lionel said no. Years later he summed it up in one sentence: I wanted to keep going, and my dad stayed with me.
The family was split between two continents. Lionel and his father in Barcelona. They lived there on part of the wage; the rest went to Rosario, for his wife and the other children.
A thirteen-year-old boy now lived eleven thousand kilometres from his mother, his brothers and his little sister.
On Sundays there was no one around. He played video games with his father at home. Afterwards, says his biographer Guillem Balagué, he went to his room to cry into his pillow.
My old man was always by my side, Messi said, and we went through a lot of ugly things together.
At the club he barely spoke. At his first training session they asked his position. He murmured one word, "forward", and sat down in a corner of the dressing room.
His teammates did not know what to think. Fàbregas said that for a long time they thought he could not speak. He could. He was just very shy. He did not talk much. He just played.
They called him "the dwarf". But when the ball came to him, nobody laughed.

Little by little he found his place. His team was full of boys born in 87, like him: Cesc Fàbregas, Gerard Piqué and others. They played with three defenders and attacked non-stop, and people started calling them the Baby Dream Team.
Over time, the quiet boy began to joke. They saw he was funny and loved cards and video games. He hated losing at those as much as at football.
In one season they hardly lost, and Messi scored more than thirty goals. Piqué, much taller, looked after him on the pitch.

His coach, Tito Vilanova, would be key in Messi's life. The story goes that one day they were winning three-nil after three minutes, and Tito joked with his assistant: what do we tell them at half-time, when we are eight-nil up?
Every night, the injection. And every year he grew a little more. In his teens, the treatment had worked.
He would be about one metre seventy. Among the shortest on any pitch. But enough.
Many years later, his doctor from Rosario, Diego Schwarzstein, said it clearly: he only helped a boy grow. Everything else Messi did.
In November 2003, Barcelona played a friendly in Porto to open a stadium. Frank Rijkaard brought on a sixteen-year-old youth player, Lionel Messi. On the other bench was José Mourinho.
It was only a friendly, but he had already played with the first team. That season he moved up through four Barça teams, one after another.
His official debut came on the sixteenth of October 2004, against Espanyol. He came on at the end, with number thirty. He was seventeen.
He was the youngest Barcelona had fielded in the Spanish league. Later others took that record from him. He would stay seventeen years at the club.
Off the pitch, people at the club say, he was so shy he barely spoke. An agent had never seen such skinny legs on a player.
But someone in the dressing room had already seen him. Ronaldinho, the best in the world, took the quiet boy under his wing.

Deco, Sylvinho and Thiago Motta, the other Brazilians, also looked after him. Ronaldinho sat next to him in the dressing room and invited him to eat at his table. Leo says he learned a lot from all of them, but above all from him.
Not everyone was so kind. The Frenchman Ludovic Giuly said some veterans kicked him in training, to see how he reacted. He never complained. He got up and kept playing.
On the first of May 2005, against Albacete, Messi came on at the end. Ronaldinho lifted a pass over the defence, and Messi chipped it over the goalkeeper. The referee called offside.
Moments later, Ronaldinho did exactly the same again. And Messi also did exactly the same again. This time, the goal counted.
Ronaldinho crouched and the boy jumped on his back. His first official goal for Barça. Ronaldinho says he is proud to have seen that story begin.

I'll pause the story for a moment. Something about me: I'm Kamil. I'm twenty-one and I've been starting YouTube channels since 2014, at nine. Almost none worked. A hundred thousand subscribers and the silver button have been my dream since I was a child. If this story means something to you, subscribing brings me one step closer. Now, back to the story.
In spring 2006, in the Champions League round of sixteen, Messi drove Chelsea crazy at Stamford Bridge. Two weeks later, in the second leg, he tore his thigh and left crying.
The whole Camp Nou stood up to applaud him. Rijkaard hugged him. Messi was eighteen.
Barcelona won the final in Paris. Messi did not play. He was so hurt that he did not join the celebrations. Years later, he said he deeply regretted that night.
Already in 2004 another question had come up. Messi had lived in Spain since he was thirteen, and the Spanish federation wanted him for its national team.
Argentina's youth coaches acted quickly. In June 2004 they set up an under-20 friendly with Paraguay, mainly so Messi would play and be tied to his country.
Argentina won eight-nil. Messi said playing for Spain was a real option. But in his heart, he was from Rosario.

Cesc Fàbregas, his friend from the academy, said it would have been amazing to see Leo with Spain. Years later, Spain won the World Cup without him. Argentina's national team would wait eleven more years for a title.

In 2005, at the Under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands, he was the best player of the tournament. He scored six goals, two of them penalties in the final against Nigeria. Argentina were world champions.
He also won the Golden Ball and the Golden Boot, as best player and top scorer. For the first time, the boy from Rosario was a champion with the albiceleste.
Six weeks later, in August 2005, he made his senior national team debut in a friendly against Hungary, in Budapest. He came on in the second half.

At his first touch, a defender grabbed his shirt. Messi pulled his arm to free himself, and the arm hit the defender. The referee showed him red. He had been on the pitch less than a minute. Reportedly, he left in tears.
Years later he said what went through his head: I came on, they sent me off, and they'll never call me again.
A teammate ran that night to protest to the referee for him. His name was Lionel Scaloni. Remember that name: years later, he would come back into this story.
But they did call him again. In March 2006, against Croatia, he scored his first goal for Argentina. And that summer he went to his first World Cup, in Germany.
Against Serbia and Montenegro he came off the bench and scored the sixth in the six-nil. At eighteen, he was the youngest Argentine to score at a World Cup.
In that match he also set up a goal for Hernán Crespo. He already looked like one of them.
In the quarter-finals, against the hosts, Germany, Argentina were winning. But the coach used his last substitutions on others, and the match slipped away. Argentina lost on penalties.
Messi stayed on the bench the whole match. For the first time, a World Cup ended and he could only watch. He did not talk to the press. Again, he said little.
In April 2007, in the Copa del Rey semi-final against Getafe, Messi took the ball in his own half. He beat one, then another, then another, then the goalkeeper, and scored.
He started on the right, near halfway. In about ten seconds he crossed almost the whole pitch with the ball glued to his left foot.
In Argentina everyone recognised that goal. It was almost the same as the one Diego Maradona, the great Argentine hero, scored against England at the 1986 World Cup. Messi was nineteen.
Barcelona won that match five-two. But in the second leg, Getafe won four-nil and knocked them out. Not even a goal like that could save his team.
They were hard years for Barça. Ronaldinho was fading, the team was losing and the club was looking for a new start. Messi improved every month, but he was often injured.

In the note he wrote after the 2026 final there is another sentence: I swear I always gave everything. And it was true. But for many years with Argentina, even giving everything was not enough to win.
In mid-2007, at the Copa América in Venezuela, Argentina reached the final against Brazil. Messi had just turned twenty. Brazil won three-nil.
He played the ninety minutes and could hardly do anything. At the end, he had to watch Brazil celebrate.
It was his first final with the senior team. Nobody knew then that he would lose three more before winning one.
In 2008 he wanted to go to the Beijing Olympics. Barcelona did not want to release him: the Games were not on the official calendar. The case went to a special sports court.
Messi said it was his decision and his only Olympic chance. The court ruled in favour of the clubs.
But Barcelona had a new coach, Pep Guardiola, Olympic gold medallist at Barcelona 1992. He understood, and let Messi go.
In Beijing he scored twice, against Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.

In the final against Nigeria, in front of about ninety thousand people, his pass put his friend Ángel Di María through alone, and he chipped the ball over the goalkeeper. It was the only goal of the match. Argentina won Olympic gold.

Later he said that in football some things happen once in a lifetime. And they were his only Games. That gold is one of the titles he values most, he has said. And in Barcelona, Guardiola was going to give him a new role.
Guardiola's first decision was a surprise: Ronaldinho, Messi's idol, was no longer in his plans. Barça would revolve around a twenty-one-year-old.
Ronaldinho left for Milan that summer. Before that, he asked Leo to take his number ten. The quiet boy who once jumped on his back now wore his number and was the team's star.
In May 2009, Barça visited Real Madrid at the Bernabéu. According to a book by Martí Perarnau, the night before Guardiola called Messi to his office and showed him a video.
Between Real's midfielders and defenders there was a gap. Guardiola asked him to start on the right and move in there, through the middle. And when he received the ball, to go straight for goal.
According to that book, Guardiola kept the plan secret until the end.
Messi played neither as a winger nor as a centre-forward. He played between both, and the defenders did not know who should follow him. Barça won six-two in Madrid. Messi scored two.
Days later, in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barça were losing in the ninety-third minute. Messi passed to Andrés Iniesta, who scored. Barça were in the final.
Three weeks later, in Rome, came the Champions League final against Manchester United. Before it, Guardiola showed them a video of the season with music from Gladiator.
Before that final, Leo remembered Paris, the night he felt left out and did not go to the celebration. This time, he said, he needed to enjoy it much more.
In the seventieth minute, Xavi crossed. And the shortest man on the pitch jumped over the defenders and headed over the giant goalkeeper, Edwin van der Sar.
Van der Sar was almost two metres tall; Messi, about one seventy. The boy who was too small beat him in the air.
Barcelona won two-nil.
That year they won everything there was. The league, the cup, the Champions League and three more titles. Six out of six, something no team had achieved before.
The sixth came in December, in Abu Dhabi, against Argentina's Estudiantes. In extra time, Messi scored the decisive goal with his chest.
Weeks earlier he won his first Ballon d'Or, the award for the best player in the world. He was twenty-two. The boy who was too small was now the best.
In January 2011, at the Ballon d'Or gala in Zurich, the three finalists came from the same school, Barcelona's academy, La Masia: Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
Almost everyone expected Xavi or Iniesta to win. They had just won the World Cup with Spain, and Iniesta scored the goal in the final. But Messi won, for the second year in a row.
He said he did not expect it, and that Xavi and Iniesta deserved it as much as he did, or more. They were the first to congratulate him.
The three gave a press conference together and said the same thing: the award belonged to the team.
Years later, Xavi remembered when he met him on a trip: a polite, humble boy, not at all big-headed. He never imagined he would be the best player in history.

In May 2011, at Wembley, Barça beat Manchester United again in a Champions League final, and Messi scored with a hard, low shot from outside the box. The most moving part came at the end. That spring, defender Éric Abidal had a tumour removed from his liver. Carles Puyol gave him the captain's armband, so that he could lift the cup.

In May 2012, Guardiola coached his last match at the Camp Nou. Messi scored all four goals, and after the fourth ran to hug him. Guardiola joked: Leo stole the spotlight all year, and he could not even be jealous of him.
In December 2012 he broke a forty-year-old record. Gerd Müller had scored eighty-five goals in one year. Messi finished the year with ninety-one, five of them in a single Champions League match.

Müller did not get angry. He called Leo a giant and joked that his only flaw was not playing for Bayern. Weeks later, Leo sent him a Barça shirt with a dedication: my respect and admiration, a hug. For Leo, titles mattered more than records.
His life off the pitch also changed. His girlfriend was Antonela Roccuzzo, a girl from Rosario he had known since childhood. In November 2012 his first son, Thiago, was born.
Two months after Thiago was born, Leo said that being a father changes you completely. His son, he said, now came first.

In January 2013 he won his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row, something no one had achieved. But Tito Vilanova was being treated for cancer again. He was his coach from La Masia, now in charge of the first team. And Abidal had just come back after a liver transplant. In his speech in Zurich, Leo forgot to thank them. Later he apologised. Tito, he once said, believed in him when Leo was a boy who was usually on the bench.
In Barcelona he was a god. With his national team, it was a different story.
Argentina had not won a major title since 1993, when Messi was six. Now a whole country wanted him to end that wait.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, Argentina's coach was Diego Maradona himself. In the quarter-finals, in Cape Town, they played Germany, who scored after three minutes and won four-nil. Messi did not score in the whole tournament.
Afterwards, Maradona said he saw Messi crying in the dressing room.
And anyone who says he does not feel this shirt, he said, is a fool.
Because that is what many people in Argentina said. He went to Spain at thirteen. He did not play for an Argentine club. He did not even sing the anthem before matches.
They had a name for players like him: "pecho frío" (cold chest). The one who does not feel enough when it counts. For many, he was quiet because he did not care.
At the 2011 Copa América, in his own country, he was booed. His father said his son was really suffering and did not understand why they whistled at him.

The coach at that Copa, Sergio Batista, wanted to use him like Barcelona did. It did not work. Messi said comparing Argentina with Barça was a mistake: the Barça players had been playing together for years.
Argentina went out in the quarter-finals, on penalties, to Uruguay. At home, the criticism did not stop. So he did what he always did. He did not talk much. He just played.

In April 2014 Tito Vilanova died, aged forty-five. Six days earlier, says a former assistant of Tito's, Leo went to see him at home and they talked for hours. The coach of his first great team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the World Cup in Brazil, Messi carried his team. After his first goal, against Bosnia, he looked at the sky, as always. He scored four in the group stage. Against Iran, the winner in the ninety-first minute.
Four times he was man of the match. Argentina were back in a World Cup final after twenty-four years.
In the semi-final they beat the Netherlands on penalties. Javier Mascherano said that without Leo, Argentina would never have got so far.
The final was at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro, again against Germany. Messi and his teammates had chances. Nobody scored. And in extra time, Mario Götze scored.
At the final whistle, Messi received the Golden Ball for the best player of the tournament. On his way to collect it, he walked right past the World Cup trophy, without looking at it.
He said the Golden Ball did not matter to him. Sepp Blatter, then FIFA president, said Messi kept repeating to himself: the best, but not the champion.
His second lost final. Three years later he said that defeat would never leave him.

In 2015, at the Copa América in Chile, Argentina reached the final again. Against Chile, it was nil-nil after a hundred and twenty minutes. Messi scored his penalty. Two teammates missed theirs, and Chile won.
Just a month earlier, with Barcelona, he had won the Champions League again, in Berlin, alongside Neymar and Luis Suárez. With his club he won everything. With his country, he kept losing.
Chile's coach in that final was the Argentine Jorge Sampaoli. Two years later, he would coach Argentina.
Afterwards, Messi wrote that there is nothing more painful in football than losing a final. He had already lost three.
Another chance came in June 2016: a special Copa América in the United States, the centenary one. The final was at MetLife Stadium, near New York.
And the opponent was Chile again. Again nobody scored. Again, it was all decided on penalties.
Messi took the first. He leaned back and the ball flew over the crossbar.
Chile won the shoot-out. It was his fourth lost final with Argentina. Three in a row, in three years.
Lucas Biglia's was also saved. But the miss that stuck was the captain's.
Minutes later, in the tunnel, a journalist stopped him. The quiet man said only: it's over, for me the national team is finished.
His teammates were devastated. Sergio Agüero, his best friend in the national team and his roommate for years, said the defeat destroyed Leo.
Messi cried on his shoulder for about twenty-five seconds, like a little child, and kept repeating the same thing: it's not for me, it's not for me.
That night, says the fitness coach, he found him awake at two in the morning, crying.

And something unexpected happened. In Argentina, people began asking him to stay. The president called him and said publicly that Messi was the greatest thing the country had. And on a rainy Saturday in Buenos Aires, hundreds of people went to the Obelisk with signs: "Don't go, Leo".
A fifteen-year-old boy, Enzo Fernández, also wrote him a letter asking him not to leave. Six years later, he would play a World Cup final at his side.
The country that called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later, he announced he was coming back. In his first match, he scored.
Why did he come back? He said he loved his country and this shirt too much, and that he wanted to help.
Later he explained why he wanted to quit: it was not only the pain of losing. There were things outside football that hurt him and his family.
And he said he did not even know whether he had told his father before saying it in the tunnel. He felt that at that moment it had to be that way.
That summer, a Spanish court convicted Messi and his father of tax fraud over his image rights. Because it was a first offence, prison was swapped for fines.
Messi stated that his father handled the money. The family had already paid back about five million euros.

In June 2017, Leo married Antonela in Rosario, the city where they grew up. He could have married anywhere, but he chose home. There were about two hundred and fifty guests, with teammates from Barça and the national team. Thiago and his little brother Mateo in the front row; his siblings signed as witnesses.

On the pitch, Argentina was struggling. Before the last round of qualifiers for Russia 2018, they were not even qualifying. They had to win in Quito, high in the Andes, where they had not won for sixteen years.

That night, in Argentina, the streets were almost empty. People watched in bars and at home. In La Plata, U2 delayed their concert so their fans could watch the match on giant screens. And in the first minute Ecuador scored. The bars went quiet.
And then Messi scored three goals. Argentina won three-one and were going to Russia. Even the Ecuadorians applauded him.
In the dressing room they sang against the critics. For Mascherano, not going to the World Cup would have been the end for many.
Messi said it would have been madness for Argentina not to go to the World Cup. Now, he said, they had peace.
His coach, Jorge Sampaoli, said something much remembered: Messi does not owe Argentina a World Cup. Football owes Messi a World Cup.
Russia did not pay that debt. In the opening match, against Iceland, Messi missed a penalty.
It was saved by Hannes Halldórsson, goalkeeper and also film director. He said he had studied Messi's penalties.
Then they lost three-nil to Croatia. They beat Nigeria with a goal from Messi, who called it a huge relief.
In the round of sixteen, against France in Kazan, Antonela came with Thiago and Mateo, who wore shirts that said Papá. Argentina lost four-three. Messi went home once again with nothing.

In his 2026 note he also wrote that leaving the national team hurt him, and still hurts deep in his soul. He had already felt that pain in Barcelona. And there, the end began with some European nights no one at the club wants to remember.

Everything was starting to break. In 2018 they thrashed Roma in the first leg and lost three-nil in Rome. A year later, the same: three-nil against Liverpool at home, and in Liverpool they lost four-nil.
After Anfield he said the coach was not to blame: it was mostly him and his teammates.
In 2019 he won his sixth Ballon d'Or, an all-time record. But that did not fix what was breaking around him.
And in August 2020, in Lisbon, Bayern Munich thrashed Barcelona eight-two.
Ten days later, Messi sent the club an official letter: he wanted to leave. Barça refused; they said his contract did not allow it.
His father flew to Barcelona to talk to the club. Messi ended up staying one more year: he would never take the club he loved to court.
Six weeks after Lisbon, Barça let Luis Suárez go, one of his best friends. Leo wrote that Suárez deserved a good farewell, not to be thrown out like that. But nothing surprised him anymore, he wrote.
In November 2020 Diego Maradona died. Argentina mourned him for days. The man who defended Messi after Cape Town was gone, and the country still had no major title with Messi.
That year, the world was locked down by the pandemic. And in 2021, the Copa América was moved to Brazil at the last moment. The final was at the Maracanã, against Brazil.
Because of the pandemic, there were hardly any fans. One of his most important matches with Argentina would be played almost in silence.
They had been away from their families for weeks. Before the final, the captain who almost never spoke stood up to talk. Someone filmed it.
For years they saw him as too quiet to be a leader. That night he found his voice.

Forty-five days without seeing family, lads, he told them. He spoke about Emiliano Martínez, the goalkeeper, who had not yet hugged his newborn daughter. And he finished: let's go out with confidence and calm, we're taking this one home.
Martínez said afterwards that he felt like crying. Another said that soon he was crying, and does not remember the rest.
After twenty-two minutes, Rodrigo De Paul played it long to Ángel Di María, the same friend from the Olympic gold. Di María chipped it over the goalkeeper. One-nil.
For seventy more minutes, Brazil attacked and Argentina held on. Messi had the chance for two-nil and missed it. It did not matter.
At the final whistle, Messi fell to his knees and covered his face. His teammates ran and piled on top of him, until he disappeared underneath.
Then he called his wife and children in Rosario. After four lost finals, he finally won a title with the national team. He was thirty-four.

Di María said the curse had to be broken one day, and it finally broke. Messi dedicated the title to his family, to the Argentines and to Maradona, who, he said, was surely cheering them on from wherever he was.
A month later he was due to renew with Barcelona. But the club announced that, because of its debts and the Spanish league's rules, it could not keep him.
On the eighth of August 2021 he walked into a room at the Camp Nou to say goodbye. Before speaking, he started to cry.
He said he was not ready. He and his family wanted to stay. He came to that city at thirteen and was leaving at thirty-four, with three sons, Thiago, Mateo and Ciro, all born there.
It hurt that he could not say goodbye to the people in the stadium. Because of the pandemic, he had not seen them for a year and a half.
He signed for Paris Saint-Germain. He never fitted in. When the team lost, he was booed.
Once, after a defeat, he travelled to Saudi Arabia for a promotional event without permission. PSG suspended him and he apologised in a video. By then everyone knew he would not stay.

In November 2022, Argentina arrived in Qatar unbeaten in thirty-six matches. Its coach was Lionel Scaloni, the teammate who defended him in Budapest. Messi was thirty-five. Everyone knew it was perhaps his last chance.
In the opening match, against Saudi Arabia, he scored a penalty. But the Saudis scored two goals in five minutes and won two-one. One of the biggest shocks in World Cup history.
Afterwards, Messi spoke to the press. No excuses, he said. The dressing room was dead. But he asked Argentines to trust the team: we will be more united than ever.
According to the players, he talked to them more than ever. The quiet captain was leading out loud.
A song followed them: "Muchachos", as the fans called it. They sang it on the bus and in the dressing room, and Messi did too.
From then on, every match was a final. Against Mexico, Messi opened the scoring and they won two-nil. Then Poland and Australia fell.
Against Australia he played the thousandth match of his career, and scored.
In the quarter-finals, against the Netherlands, Argentina were winning two-nil, and the Dutch equalised in the last seconds. There were penalties, and Argentina won.

After that match, the world saw a Messi it did not know. In the middle of an interview a Dutch player walked past, and Messi shot at him, the way people talk on the streets of Rosario: "What are you looking at, silly?"

The one they called cold now had a burning chest. In the semi-final, three-nil against Croatia. Messi scored a penalty and then beat one of the best young defenders in the world to set up a goal for Julián Álvarez.
On the eighteenth of December 2022, Argentina played the final against France. Messi scored a penalty. Di María got the second.
Two-nil, ten minutes from the end. Four lost finals behind, and the cup right there.
And in less than two minutes, Kylian Mbappé scored twice. Two-two.
Extra time. Messi scored again: three-two. And then Mbappé scored again, from the penalty spot. Three-three.
In the last minute, Martínez stopped a French chance with his leg. And after a hundred and twenty minutes, the World Cup went to penalties.
Messi scored his. Martínez saved one, and France missed another. And it was Gonzalo Montiel's turn, with the penalty that could give them everything.
We are back at the start of this documentary. Montiel went to the ball. Messi looked at the sky; he later said he was asking God for it to be over.
Montiel scores. Lionel Messi fell to his knees on the grass.
He had lost four finals with Argentina. He had said enough. He had come back. And now, at thirty-five, he was world champion.
Before lifting the trophy, the Emir of Qatar put a traditional black robe on him. Then he raised the cup, kissed it and would not let go of it.
His family came onto the pitch. His mother hugged him. His three sons ran to him, and he photographed Antonela with the cup.

His goals in the final were his sixth and seventh of the tournament. He won the Golden Ball again, the award that eight years earlier did not matter to him because they lost. This time he also had the cup.
At that World Cup he was the first player to score in the group stage, round of sixteen, quarter-final, semi-final and final.
Later, in an interview, he said he heard the cup calling him, as if saying: now, yes, touch me.
He never watched the final again, he said, only highlights. At home, his sons imitated goalkeeper Martínez's celebrations.
In Buenos Aires, millions filled the streets. There were so many that the bus could not move and the players left by helicopter.

In March 2023, before leaving Europe, he had another happy night in Buenos Aires. In the first home match as world champions, against Panama at the Monumental, he scored the eight-hundredth goal of his career. He said he had always dreamed of this: celebrating with his people, at home.

That summer, when his contract in Paris ended, he surprised everyone. Not Barça, not the huge offer from Saudi Arabia. He chose a young club in the United States, Inter Miami. Many thought he was going to slow down.
He explained it simply: he wanted to step out of the spotlight a bit and think more about his family. If it were for money, he said, he would have gone to Saudi Arabia.
His first match for Miami was in July 2023. He came on in the second half. In the ninety-fourth minute, at one-one, he curled a free kick into the top corner.
That night he smiled from the bench at Antonela and his three sons in the stands. LeBron James and Serena Williams were there too. With the goal, David Beckham, the club's co-owner, cried.
Weeks later, Miami won its first title. No slowing down. And in October came his eighth Ballon d'Or.
In Miami he was also a football dad. His three sons joined the academy, and he and Antonela cheered them on from the sideline, like any parent.
In 2024, Argentina reached another Copa América final, against Colombia, in Miami. In the second half he twisted his ankle and had to come off.

On the bench, he cried. His teammate Leandro Paredes sat next to him. He said he could not even look at him, only hear him cry. Argentina won in extra time without him. It was the last match of his friend Di María.

In September 2025 he played what, he said, would perhaps be his last home qualifier, against Venezuela in Buenos Aires. In the warm-up he was nearly crying, while more than eighty thousand people chanted his name. He scored two goals. Ending like that, at home, he said, was what he had always dreamed of.
In December 2025, Miami won its first MLS Cup. On the pitch, his son Mateo juggled the ball and pointed at his father.
In March 2026 he scored the nine-hundredth goal of his career. He was thirty-eight, and some already saw him as old.
It was in a match Miami did not win and that knocked them out of a continental cup. The result mattered more to him than the record. And another World Cup was coming.
His father, Jorge, had always wanted to see him play one more World Cup. But just before the tournament, Jorge fell seriously ill. For the first time, Jorge would not be there to watch him.
In the first match, against Algeria, he scored three goals. Then two against Austria and one against Jordan. Argentina won their group without trouble.
And after every match, the same thing. Boots off. Phone in hand. Any message from home? That way he would know how his father was.
He did not say it then, but he was playing with his father ill thousands of kilometres away. And later he admitted he never felt well during the tournament.
In the knockouts, every match was a battle. Against Cape Verde there was extra time.

Against Egypt, Messi missed a penalty. He did not hang his head. He set up a goal for Cristian Romero, equalised himself, and Enzo Fernández won the match with a header. Against Switzerland, extra time again.
Boots off. Phone. A message from home?
In the semi-final, in Atlanta, England scored first. Argentina came back in the last five minutes, and in the last one, Messi delivered the winning cross. Two-one. In the final again.
When it ended, Messi was very emotional. Then he went around the pitch hugging teammates and staff. Even Scaloni was left speechless.
He had scored eight goals at that World Cup. No one in history scored more World Cup goals, or played more matches.
The final was on the nineteenth of July 2026, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The same stadium where, ten years earlier, he said it was over.
In the dressing room, before the final, he asked them for calm: forget everything else and think only about playing.
Spain had nineteen-year-old Lamine Yamal and a young team. It dominated the ball and had almost all the chances.
It was still nil-nil. In a video published later, Messi can be heard telling the team: character, everyone, character.
At the end of the ninety minutes Enzo Fernández, the boy with the letter, was sent off. Ten against eleven and half an hour to hold on.
In the hundred-and-sixth minute, Ferran Torres scored. Argentina could not respond.
Messi had only one shot in the whole match. His fifth lost final with Argentina.

After the final whistle, Messi sat on the grass. Yamal went to hug him. Messi told him to keep going his way, that the future belonged to his generation. For Yamal, those words were worth a gold medal.
Scaloni broke down in front of the press and had to leave. Before the final, he had said Messi was the best player ever to step on a pitch.
And the next day, Messi wrote to the fans. The pain is immense, he said, and this wound will take time to heal.
In August 2026, less than three weeks after the final, Jorge died in Rosario, after a long illness. He was sixty-eight.
Days later, Lionel wrote him a letter and made it public. It began with a simple sentence. I love you, dad.

He wrote that he promised his father to reach the final, so that he could go and see it. His father did not make it. Lionel wanted to win it and bring him the cup. But he could not, he wrote. His legs had nothing left.
And he wrote that at the World Cup, after every match, he waited for a message from his father. When it did not come, he understood how serious it was.
You were my dad, my friend and my agent, he wrote. The same man who left Rosario and waited in Barcelona for a napkin.
From then on, when he looked at the sky, he saw two people.
On the thirty-first of August, Messi published the note from the beginning. He had written it on the twenty-first of July, two days after the final, and kept it for six weeks.
In it he said goodbye to the national team. I emptied myself, he wrote. I have nothing left to give, and great young players are coming who deserve their place. Now I will be one more of you.
Later, he added a line at the end: today, after what happened with my dad, I am even more sure of my decision.
He did not write about titles or finals. He wrote about his family, the people and his father.

On the sixth of October 2026 he played his last match for Argentina, a friendly against Benin, at the Monumental in Buenos Aires. It was River Plate's stadium. The club that once wanted that boy from Rosario and could not have him.
About eighty-five thousand people came. He walked out holding his three sons' hands. His mother watched from the stands.
The anthem was sung by a veteran of the Falklands War. Messi was almost crying. In the tenth minute, everything stopped for a long ovation, and the Benin players went over to him.
He gave two assists and then scored a penalty. It was his hundred-and-twenty-sixth goal for Argentina, in his two-hundred-and-eighth match.
The second went to Nico Paz, twenty-two, one of the young players who, he said, deserved their place.
Afterwards, hundreds of drones lit up the sky. And the boy who used to sit quietly in a corner of the dressing room took the microphone in front of eighty-five thousand.
First he said he was thinking of his father. Then, that it was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks there was argument about the referees at that World Cup. Messi stayed out of it. That night he said nothing strange happened. His team simply gave everything.
He said playing for Argentina was the most beautiful thing that can happen to anyone, and that he would like to be there forever. And he told them he loved them and would miss them.
Then he did a lap with his wife and sons, while eighty-five thousand sang that Messi is not leaving.
He called it the saddest day of his career. And yet, in his note, he had written: I leave in peace and with pride.
He was too small. Too expensive. A foreigner in Spain and a stranger in Argentina. Later they said he was too old.
But two people did not. A grandmother who asked for him to be put on, and a father who gathered the money, crossed the sea with him and stayed.
He never played only for himself. He played for them. And when he looks at the sky after a goal, it is them he is looking for.
The cold chest Argentina talked about was never cold. He just did not show what he felt. He kept it inside, and let it out when he lost, or when he finally won.
And that last final, in July 2026, hurt more than any other. It was not just another title. It was the last thing he wanted to bring his father.
Today he still plays in Miami. He has scored more than nine hundred goals. He no longer plays for Argentina. Now, as he wrote, he is just one more fan.
Maybe you are the quiet one. The one in the corner. The one they think cares about nothing.
Leo was that boy too. He never became loud. He did not talk much. He just played, for those who believed in him. And when it mattered most, he found his voice. One day, the whole world heard him.
If you are the quiet one, you don't need to shout. Keep playing. Your time to speak will come.
And the night he said goodbye to Argentina, the boy who hardly spoke smiled at eighty-five thousand people. I'm talking more than ever, he said, and I don't want to leave.
That summer, Spain did not only end Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks earlier, in Texas, it had broken the dream of another boy, who wanted that cup as much as he did.
A boy from a small island in the Atlantic, whom his teammates called crybaby. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his full story is here.
